parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Define electric field strength at a point, including its direction.

answer.text: Electric field strength is the electric force per unit positive test charge placed at that point: E=F/q. Its direction is that of the force on a positive test charge, sufficiently small not to disturb the original field.

evidence.review: Derived independently from the question and checked against the first-assessment2025 IB Physics guide; handwritten annotations are not answer evidence.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Two point charges R and S lie at x=0 and x=5.0 cm. The graph shows the resultant electric field component along the positive x direction between them. (a) Determine the sign of each charge. (b) Use the zero-field position to find |S|/|R|.

answer.text: (a) Both charges are negative: near R the field points toward R, while near S it points toward S. (b) The zero occurs at x≈2.0 cm, so the distances are 2.0 cm from R and 3.0 cm from S. Equating field magnitudes gives k|R|/2²=k|S|/3², hence |S|/|R|=9/4=2.25, about 2.

parts.display_text: Two bar magnets have their opposite poles facing as shown. A small freely turning magnet is placed at X without significantly disturbing the field. Describe how to draw its orientation and label its north and south poles.

answer.text: Draw the small magnet tangent to the field line at X. The external field points away from the large north pole, along the curve toward the upper right at X, so the small magnet’s north end points upper right and its south end lower left.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Two parallel horizontal plates are separated by 3.0 cm and have a potential difference of 14 V. The upper plate is positive and the lower plate is negative. Neglect edge effects. Find the electric field strength and its direction between them.

answer.text: The uniform field magnitude is E=V/d=14/0.030=4.67×10² N C⁻¹. It points downward, from the positive upper plate toward the negative lower plate.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Two horizontal parallel wires lie in the page. The upper wire carries current to the right and the lower wire carries current to the left. Point A lies between them. The individual field magnitudes at A are given: 2B₀ from the upper wire and B₀ from the lower wire. What is the resultant field at A?

A. B₀ into the page
B. B₀ out of the page
C. 3B₀ into the page
D. 3B₀ out of the page

answer.text: C. The right-hand grip rule gives a field into the page below the upper wire and into the page above the lower wire. They add to 3B₀ into the page.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
An isolated conducting sphere in vacuum has radius 0.62 m and charge +83 pC.

(a) Define electric field strength at a point.
(b) Sketch the electric field lines outside the sphere.
(c) Calculate the surface field strength, using k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², and give a unit.

answer.text:
(a) Electric force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q.
(b) Draw symmetrically spaced radial lines perpendicular to the surface, with arrowheads pointing outwards.
(c) E = kQ/r² = (8.99 × 10⁹)(83 × 10⁻¹²)/(0.62)² = 1.94 N C⁻¹ ≈ 1.9 N C⁻¹.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
The diagram models Earth’s magnetic field using a solenoid along a tilted magnetic axis. Two field arrows are already shown.

(a) Identify the magnetic north and south ends.
(b) Complete a qualitative sketch of the external magnetic field.
(c) Describe how field strength and direction relative to the local surface vary between the magnetic equator and magnetic poles.

answer.text:
(a) The upper end is magnetic south, because the exterior field enters there; the lower end is magnetic north, because the field emerges there.
(b) Draw continuous curved lines from the lower north end to the upper south end, with the usual solenoid/bar-magnet pattern and no crossings.
(c) The field is strongest and approximately normal to the surface near the magnetic poles. It is weaker and approximately parallel to the surface near the magnetic equator; the inclination changes continuously between these regions.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
An electron initially at rest at plate X accelerates towards parallel plate Y when a potential difference of 58 kV is applied. The plate separation is 0.041 m.

(a) Identify the positive and negative plates.
(b) Calculate the uniform field strength between the plates, giving its direction and a unit.

answer.text:
(a) X is negative and Y is positive: a negative electron is attracted towards Y.
(b) E = V/d = 58 000/0.041 = 1.41 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹, directed from Y to X. N C⁻¹ is an equivalent unit.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Which is not a possible charge on a charge carrier?

A. −4.8×10⁻¹⁹ C
B. −2.4×10⁻¹⁹ C
C. +1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C
D. +3.2×10⁻¹⁹ C

answer.text:
Official key B checked; editorial worked explanation:

B. Charge is quantized in integer multiples of e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. The magnitudes in A, C and D are 3e, e and 2e. Option B is 1.5e, not an integer multiple.

evidence.detail: Cambridge 9702/12 May/June 2024 published key B, PDF page 3; explanation is editorial.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: An initially uncharged oil drop gains charge +4.0×10⁻¹⁸ C. What change occurs? A. gained 25 electrons  B. gained 64 electrons  C. lost 25 electrons  D. lost 64 electrons

answer.text: Official answer C. Editorial worked explanation: The number of elementary charges is N=Q/e=(4.0×10⁻¹⁸)/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹)=25. A positive change means negative charge was removed, so the drop lost 25 electrons.
answer.evidence: OCR H156/01 June 2023 markscheme checked on PDF page 9; editorial explanation independently recalculated.

fast-ib-production-001-a-nov-q21:whole.hint: Apply the right-hand grip rule to each wire separately at R, then add the two field vectors.
notes: Opposite current directions do not make the fields cancel because R lies in different directions from the wires.
Equal distance and equal current make the two perpendicular magnetic-field contributions equal in magnitude.

original-ib26mb2-written-4-a:whole.hint: Identify the force-to-charge ratio and the test-charge convention that defines the vector direction.
notes: Force and field are different quantities. The same field exerts forces of different magnitude on different charges.
The sign of the test charge matters for direction: a negative charge experiences a force opposite to the electric field.

original-ib26mb2-written-4-b-c:whole.hint: Use the direction of the field near each charge to find its sign. At the crossing of the axis, the two field magnitudes cancel.
notes: A field zero between two point charges requires like signs. The field component on each side of the zero then distinguishes two negative charges from two positive ones.
The larger charge must be farther from the zero to produce the same field magnitude. Remember the inverse square, not inverse distance, dependence.

original-ib26mb2-written-9-a:whole.hint: First establish the external field direction near the labelled north pole, then follow the tangent at X.
notes: A small magnet aligns along the local field, not necessarily along a straight line to the large pole. Use the curve’s direction exactly at X.
The north-seeking end points in the field direction. Outside a magnet, field lines leave north and enter south.

original-ib26mc2-written-6-ai:whole.hint: Use the plate separation in metres. Determine direction from the positive-test-charge convention.
notes: The 14 V is a potential difference, not a force or an energy. Dividing by separation gives V m⁻¹, equivalent to N C⁻¹.
Neglecting edge effects is what permits the uniform parallel-plate relation. Field direction is independent of the sign of any particular moving particle.

cross-aq24p2-25:whole.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

cross-aq24p2-27:whole.hint: For the ion to remain suspended, how must its electric force compare with its weight?
notes: Equilibrium requires |q|E = mg. First choose the electric-force direction to balance weight, then account for the sign of the charge when stating the field direction.

cross-vc23-2:whole.hint: Work out the direction of each electric-field contribution using a positive test charge.
notes: For a point charge, |E| = k|Q|/r² and force is F = qE. Add fields as vectors; a negative test charge experiences force opposite the field.
Unlike charges attract and like charges repel. Keep source charge, test charge and their separation distinct when using Coulomb’s law.

cross-ap2ced-mcq-10:whole.hint: Determine each field direction independently before adding their magnitudes.
notes: Opposite current directions do not automatically mean opposite fields at a point. Position relative to each wire matters.

cross-ca25n42-written-6-a-bi-biv:whole.hint: Outside a charged sphere, spherical symmetry allows its field to be treated like that of a point charge at its centre.
notes: Use the sphere’s radius for the distance to its surface. Positive charge gives outward field arrows. The test charge in the definition should be small enough not to disturb the field.

cross-ca25j42-written-2-bi-bii-cii:whole.hint: Use the existing field-arrow directions, rather than assigning magnetic polarity from a geographic label.
notes: Outside a magnet, field lines run from magnetic north to south; the lines form closed loops through the interior. Field-line spacing indicates relative strength.
This is a supplied solenoid model. Geographic north and a magnetic north pole are not interchangeable labels.

cross-ca25j42-written-6-a-bi:whole.hint: An electric field points in the direction of force on a positive charge. The electron is negative.
notes: Field and electron acceleration point in opposite directions. Convert kV to V before dividing by the plate separation.

cross-fast-vcaa-85b84de5ad48f3e7-1-whole.hint: Convert both quantities to SI units before dividing potential difference by plate separation.
notes: Between ideal parallel plates the field is approximately uniform away from the edges.
A millimetre-to-metre conversion changes the denominator by a factor of one thousand.

cross-fast-production-004-a-q33:whole.hint: Divide each charge magnitude by the elementary charge and look for a non-integer result.
notes: The sign may be positive or negative; quantization constrains the magnitude to integer multiples of e.
The value 2.4×10⁻¹⁹ C equals 1.5e, so it cannot be the net charge of an isolated carrier.

cross-fast-ocr-9b5d09d08cd2c050-20-whole.hint: Divide the charge magnitude by the elementary charge, then use the sign to decide whether electrons were gained or lost.
notes: Removing electrons leaves a positive net charge; adding electrons would make the drop negative.
Electric charge is quantized, so the result is an integer multiple of the elementary charge.
